---
title: "Calculate metrics"
description: "Turn clean positions into speed, direction of travel, body heading and distance travelled, then summarise them."
order: 5
---



Positions are rarely the answer to a research question. Speed, distance
travelled, and how much an animal turned and when usually are.
[animetric](https://animovement.dev/animetric) derives them from a clean
anipoint. We start from the pipeline in the [previous guide](process-data.qmd),
with one addition: angles in degrees rather than radians, which are easier to
read.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(animovement)

clean <- read_dataset(get_sample_data("sleap")) |>
  set_metadata(sampling_rate = 30) |>
  convert_unit_time("s") |>
  convert_unit_space("cm", calibration_factor = 9 / 140) |>
  convert_unit_angle("deg") |>
  mask_na_across("roi", x_min = 19, x_max = 65, y_min = 0, y_max = 45) |>
  mask_na_across("confidence", threshold = 0.6) |>
  replace_na_across("linear", max_gap = 5) |>
  filter_across("sgolay", window_width = 11, order = 3)
```
:::


## Kinematics {#sec-kinematics}

`add_kinematics()` adds a column for each derived quantity. There's nothing
to configure: it reads the coordinate system, the sampling rate, the angle unit
and the grouping from the metadata.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
kinematics <- add_kinematics(clean)

setdiff(names(kinematics), names(clean))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>  [1] "speed"                "acceleration"         "cumulative_distance" 
#>  [4] "v_x"                  "v_y"                  "a_x"                 
#>  [7] "a_y"                  "course"               "course_unwrapped"    
#> [10] "turning_speed"        "turning_rate"         "turning_acceleration"
#> [13] "cumulative_turning"
```


:::
:::


The new columns come in two families:

- **How fast:** `speed`, `acceleration` (how fast the speed changes),
  `cumulative_distance` (the distance travelled so far), and the velocity and
  acceleration along each axis, `v_x`, `v_y`, `a_x` and `a_y`.
- **Which way:** `course`, the direction of travel, and how it changes:
  `turning_rate`, `turning_speed`, `turning_acceleration`, and
  `cumulative_turning`. `course_unwrapped` is the same direction without the
  jump from 180° to −180°.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
kinematics
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # Individuals:   individual1
#> # Keypoints:     centre, left_ear, right_ear, snout, tail_base, tail_end
#> # Sampling rate: 30 Hz
#> # Time:          00:00:00 to 00:10:16
#>    individual  keypoint   time     x     y confidence speed acceleration
#>    <fct>       <fct>     <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>      <dbl> <dbl>        <dbl>
#>  1 individual1 centre   0.0333    NA    NA         NA    NA           NA
#>  2 individual1 centre   0.0667    NA    NA         NA    NA           NA
#>  3 individual1 centre   0.1       NA    NA         NA    NA           NA
#>  4 individual1 centre   0.133     NA    NA         NA    NA           NA
#>  5 individual1 centre   0.167     NA    NA         NA    NA           NA
#>  6 individual1 centre   0.2       NA    NA         NA    NA           NA
#>  7 individual1 centre   0.233     NA    NA         NA    NA           NA
#>  8 individual1 centre   0.267     NA    NA         NA    NA           NA
#>  9 individual1 centre   0.3       NA    NA         NA    NA           NA
#> 10 individual1 centre   0.333     NA    NA         NA    NA           NA
#> # i 110,900 more rows
#> # i 11 more variables: cumulative_distance <dbl>, v_x <dbl>, v_y <dbl>,
#> #   a_x <dbl>, a_y <dbl>, course <dbl>, course_unwrapped <dbl>,
#> #   turning_speed <dbl>, turning_rate <dbl>, turning_acceleration <dbl>,
#> #   cumulative_turning <dbl>
```


:::
:::


A direction of travel only means something when the point actually moves.
While the mouse sits still, tracking noise still moves its keypoints a fraction
of a pixel, and the direction between two such positions is random. So below a
minimum step, `min_step`, a row gets no `course` and adds nothing to the
turning measures. By default it's estimated from each track's own noise, which
is cautious. To be stricter, set it in the frame's units, for example
`add_kinematics(clean, min_step = 0.1)` for a millimetre.

::: {.callout-important}
## Check your units before you believe a number
Speed here is in **centimetres per second**, because we
[converted both units](read-data.qmd#sec-metadata) when reading the data. Every
one of these numbers is only as good as those two conversions: get the
sampling rate or the spatial scale wrong, and every speed is off by the same
factor.
:::

## Look at it {#sec-plot}

`plot_timeseries()` draws a column against time:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
kinematics |>
  dplyr::filter(keypoint == "centre") |>
  plot_timeseries(variable = "speed")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Speed of the mouse's centre over ten minutes, in centimetres per second.](calculate-metrics_files/figure-html/speed-plot-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


Bursts of movement separated by long still stretches: the pattern you'd expect
from a mouse exploring a plus maze. A spike that looks too sudden to be real is
worth going back to mask, with the `"speed"` or `"hampel"` method of
`mask_na_across()`, rather than explaining away.

## Where it goes and where it faces {#sec-heading}

`course` is the direction a point is *moving*. That isn't always the direction
the animal is *facing*: a mouse can turn its body while barely moving, and
when it stops, there is no direction of travel at all.

Where the body points is its orientation, and `add_orientation()` works it out
from two points. Here, the line from the base of the tail to the snout gives
the mouse's heading:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
oriented <- clean |>
  add_orientation(from = "tail_base", to = "snout", level = "keypoint") |>
  add_kinematics()
```
:::


The heading is attached to every keypoint, since it belongs to the body as a
whole. Over one second of a run, the two directions start apart while the
mouse turns, then come together as it runs straight:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
oriented |>
  dplyr::filter(keypoint == "centre", time > 100, time < 101) |>
  dplyr::select(time, speed, course, heading)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # Individuals:   individual1
#> # Keypoints:     centre
#> # Sampling rate: 30 Hz
#> # Time:          00:01:40.033 to 00:01:40.967
#>    individual  keypoint  time speed course heading
#>    <fct>       <fct>    <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>
#>  1 individual1 centre    100.  13.9  -173.   -140.
#>  2 individual1 centre    100.  16.1  -170.   -148.
#>  3 individual1 centre    100.  16.6  -168.   -156.
#>  4 individual1 centre    100.  16.2  -169.   -163.
#>  5 individual1 centre    100.  17.4  -171.   -169.
#>  6 individual1 centre    100.  18.7  -172.   -174.
#>  7 individual1 centre    100.  17.9  -173.   -177.
#>  8 individual1 centre    100.  16.6  -177.   -179.
#>  9 individual1 centre    100.  15.9   178.    180.
#> 10 individual1 centre    100.  14.2   174.    180.
#> # i 19 more rows
```


:::
:::


Over the whole recording, a circular plot shows where each direction points.
Weighting `course` by speed lets the runs count for more than the shuffles:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
centre <- dplyr::filter(oriented, keypoint == "centre")

plots(
  plot_circular(centre, variable = "course", weight = "speed"),
  plot_circular(centre, variable = "heading")
)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Directions over ten minutes: where the mouse's centre travelled (left, weighted by speed) and where its body pointed (right). The line marks the mean direction.](calculate-metrics_files/figure-html/rose-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


The direction of travel follows the four arms of the maze: that's the only
way to go. The body's heading follows them too, but it also points along the
diagonals, from the moments when the mouse sits nearly still and turns to look
around. Those moments have no direction of travel at all, so only the heading
can show them.

## Summarise {#sec-summarise}

Per-frame kinematics are the raw material; usually you want one row per track.
animetric has two kinds of summary.

`summarise_aniframe()` summarises the distribution of each per-frame measure.
It defaults to the median and the median absolute deviation (MAD), because
movement data is rarely symmetric enough for a mean and standard deviation to
describe it well. Angles such as `course` and `heading` get circular
statistics, so the average of 350° and 10° comes out as 0°, not 180°.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
summarise_aniframe(oriented)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 6 x 18
#>   individual  keypoint  median_speed mad_speed median_acceleration
#>   <fct>       <fct>            <dbl>     <dbl>               <dbl>
#> 1 individual1 centre            2.55      2.44              0.0632
#> 2 individual1 left_ear          4.54      4.41             -0.210 
#> 3 individual1 right_ear         4.58      4.39             -0.325 
#> 4 individual1 snout             6.63      6.00             -0.857 
#> 5 individual1 tail_base         2.54      2.62             -0.0641
#> 6 individual1 tail_end          2.19      2.69              0.0217
#> # i 13 more variables: mad_acceleration <dbl>, median_turning_speed <dbl>,
#> #   mad_turning_speed <dbl>, median_turning_rate <dbl>, mad_turning_rate <dbl>,
#> #   median_turning_acceleration <dbl>, mad_turning_acceleration <dbl>,
#> #   median_confidence <dbl>, mad_confidence <dbl>, median_course <dbl>,
#> #   mad_course <dbl>, median_heading <dbl>, mad_heading <dbl>
```


:::
:::


There's one row per keypoint, since that's how this recording is grouped. The
snout moves fastest: it swings as the mouse turns its head, so it covers more
ground than the body it's attached to. Pass `measures = "mean_sd"` if you'd
rather have the mean and standard deviation.

`summarise_path()` describes each track's path as a whole: the total distance,
the total turning, how far the animal ended up from where it started, and how
straight or winding the path was:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
summarise_path(clean)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 6 x 8
#>   individual keypoint total_distance total_turning net_displacement straightness
#>   <fct>      <fct>             <dbl>         <dbl>            <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1 individua~ centre            2510.       243452.            22.1       0.00880
#> 2 individua~ left_ear          3489.       201938.            20.0       0.00573
#> 3 individua~ right_e~          3445.       203603.            14.0       0.00405
#> 4 individua~ snout             3135.       140416.            22.1       0.00704
#> 5 individua~ tail_ba~          2420.       223257.            23.2       0.00960
#> 6 individua~ tail_end          2029.       211706.             5.33      0.00263
#> # i 2 more variables: sinuosity <dbl>, e_max <dbl>
```


:::
:::


## Beyond kinematics {#sec-more}

The same anipoint feeds the rest of animetric:

- `add_point()` adds a point derived from others, such as the centroid of the
  head from the snout and both ears.
- `add_tortuosity()` measures how winding a path is over sliding windows.
- `calculate_nnd()` finds the distance to the nearest neighbour, for
  recordings with several individuals.

When the question is about space rather than time,
[anispace](https://animovement.dev/anispace) transforms the coordinates
themselves. `transform_to_egocentric()` re-expresses positions from the
animal's own point of view, `map_to_polar()` and related functions change the
coordinate system, and `rotate_coords()` and `translate_coords()` align
recordings with each other.
